Volkswagen's Wolfsburg Retreat Meets a Chinese Sales Surge as Union Talks Loom
sum: Volkswagen has shelved the "Gamechanger" production concept at its Wolfsburg headquarters, abandoning the planned form of the project along with the large casting plant earmarked for it. The decision, reported by Reuters on Wednesday, forms part of a group-wide review of investments as the carmaker confronts a strained economic climate.

The retreat at home contrasts with progress elsewhere. On Thursday the company confirmed the start of series production of the fully electric ID. Tiguan at its Emden plant. The model succeeds the ID.4, with dealers due to receive it at the beginning of 2027.

Product recognition has also been rolling in. Volkswagen said on Wednesday that the ID. Polo has collected the "Goldene Lenkrad" award and the "Autonis" design prize, adding the "German Car of the Year 2027" title to its haul.

In China, the picture is more mixed. Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing two informants, that no new models are planned for Volkswagen Anhui in 2027 and 2028. Volkswagen China responded that its focus is on expanding and optimising its dealer network — a statement that addresses distribution rather than the model plan itself.

Yet the brand's electrified lineup is gaining real traction in the world's largest car market. Volkswagen China reported around 28,000 deliveries for October, a jump of roughly 347% from the same month a year earlier. Whether that momentum can be converted into earnings is the open question.

The backdrop to all of this is a hefty hit to the bottom line. On 29 October Volkswagen posted a net loss of EUR 5.82 billion for the third quarter of 2026. Management has guided for a full-year operating margin of up to 1% on revenue of around EUR 315 billion — a wafer-thin cushion that leaves little room for error.

That is why the looming labour dispute matters so much to the investment case. Layoffs have inflamed tensions ahead of the wage round, and the first negotiating session is scheduled for 24 November, according to media reports. A negotiated framework could smooth the path for cost cuts; a hardening of positions would make them harder to deliver.

sum: Volkswagen is scaling back a major manufacturing project at its Wolfsburg headquarters as weaker earnings force the automaker to rethink investment across its German factories. The decision, announced on Wednesday, November 11, keeps the next-generation electric platform and planned models such as the ID. Roc in focus, but abandons the Gamechanger concept in the form previously planned, according to Bloomberg via Yahoo Finance.

Volkswagen stock traded at 67.59 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:14 CET on Friday, November 13, 2026, 0.19 percent below the Xetra close of Thursday, November 12. The comparison puts the latest indication slightly below the previous completed Xetra session while investors assess whether the group's restructuring can protect future competitiveness.

The Wolfsburg project was intended to introduce new production methods that could later be used more widely across the group. One element was gigacasting, which uses very large presses to produce substantial body sections with fewer parts and manufacturing steps. Volkswagen said work on its new electric platform and planned vehicles would continue despite the change.

Daniela Cavallo, head of Volkswagen's works council, called the decision a breach of a December 2024 agreement and criticized the retreat from advanced manufacturing. She also said labor would resist moving combustion-engine Golf production from Wolfsburg to Mexico until management explains the consequences for jobs and factory volumes. The transfer is planned for next year to create capacity for future electric models.

That dispute comes as Volkswagen seeks to reduce capacity and costs in Germany. The company is targeting roughly 100,000 job cuts worldwide and has raised the possibility of closing German plants. The strong role of employee representatives on Volkswagen's supervisory board makes negotiations a central factor in the pace and scope of the overhaul.

Volkswagen's investor information shows that revenue for the first nine months of 2026 fell to 233.4 billion euros from 238.7 billion euros a year earlier. Operating result dropped to 0.1 billion euros from 5.4 billion euros. Before special items, operating result was 8.8 billion euros and the operating return on sales was 3.8 percent.

sum: Volkswagen is abandoning its planned Gamechanger manufacturing concept at its Wolfsburg headquarters in the form originally intended, Bloomberg reported through Automotive News on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The decision marks a retreat from a major factory-modernization project as weaker earnings force the German carmaker to reassess investment across its domestic plants.

The report says Volkswagen will continue work on its next-generation electric platform and planned models including the ID. Roc. The company is therefore not abandoning future electric vehicles, but is narrowing the manufacturing ambitions attached to them at Wolfsburg.

That distinction matters for investors. Scrapping the project can conserve capital and reduce execution risk while Volkswagen works to restore profitability. It also raises questions about how quickly the group can modernize production, lower unit costs and prepare its German factories for a more electric product mix.

Works council chief Daniela Cavallo described the decision as a breach of a December 2024 agreement, according to the report. She also opposed moving combustion-engine Golf production from Wolfsburg to Mexico until Volkswagen explains the consequences for jobs and factory volumes.

The dispute adds a labor dimension to the restructuring. Management is seeking a leaner industrial footprint, while employee representatives want clarity on production commitments and employment. Any delay in implementing factory changes could weaken the savings case, but a faster reduction in German capacity could increase operational and political resistance.

For the shares, the key issue is whether lower investment spending can improve financial flexibility without slowing the product rollout. The next milestones are management's implementation plans for Wolfsburg, negotiations with labor representatives and evidence that new electric models can support margins rather than add to the group's cost burden.

sum: Volkswagen has won the EU Commission's blessing to take sole control of Europcar Mobility, but the green light from Brussels did little to lift sentiment on the stock. The shares were down 2.2% at €69.04 on the day, with the market's attention fixed less on regulatory approval than on whether the rental business can be made to pay.

The Commission raised no competition objections, according to media reports, and reviewed the merger under its simplified procedure given the limited impact on market structure. Volkswagen has held a majority stake in Europcar since buying it back in 2022 and now moves to full ownership. The regulatory path is clear; the economic one is not.

Under the deal, Volkswagen is acquiring Attestor's stake for roughly €1 billion, lifting its indirect holding to 93%, while Pon keeps its share. Sole control and remaining minority interests can therefore sit side by side. Europcar's revenue came in at €3,320 million in 2025, a decline of 2.5% — a business that must first repair its earnings before it can add anything to the group.

The strategic case rests on scale and reach. Europcar operates about 270,000 vehicles across more than 130 countries, and Volkswagen intends to fold the rental arm into a broader mobility offering: customers would hire, subscribe to or share cars through a single app. According to Handelsblatt, that expansion was already part of the planned strategy, and full control could make it easier to execute. Europcar is also earmarked as a sales channel for the group's own vehicles — a potential double benefit, provided the combination carries its weight financially.

Those ambitions are being pursued against a grim set of numbers. On 29 October, Volkswagen reported a net loss of €5.8 billion for the third quarter of 2026. As AP reported, a €6.4 billion impairment tied to Porsche weighed on the result, alongside weak demand in China, US tariffs and lower profits from electric vehicles.

The Core brand group also lost ground. Its operating result for the first nine months of 2026 reached €4.33 billion, down from €4.72 billion a year earlier, while the operating margin slipped to 4.1% from 4.4%. At group level, third-quarter revenue of €75.28 billion was 6.26% below the prior-year period, and the loss per share came to €9.24.

Did Volkswagen's Fall Catch You Out? What Bears Saw
sum: Volkswagen spent most of 2026 in the headlines for profit warnings, restructuring plans and rising tariff pressure, yet the real shock for many investors sat in their account statements. For Volkswagen shareholders, the loss from the start of the year was 30.0%, including dividends. If you had been weighing up a position on 1 January, with bullish and bearish analysts already far apart, which early signals about profitability resilience would you have focused on?
The useful thing about a Narrative is that the reasoning is checkable: the assumptions sit beside the argument, and together they imply an estimated Fair Value you can disagree with.
The shares cost €104 at the start of the period, and Volkswagen sat between two very different stories about what might happen next.

On the optimistic side, the bullish narrative saw fair value at €114. It rested on revenue growing 2.8% a year and profit margins reaching 4.5%, helped by electric and plug-in hybrid expansion and new digital services.

The bearish view put fair value at €90. That case focused on a possible 0.5% annual revenue decline and pressure from rising compliance costs, mobility as a service, and geopolitics eroding margins over time.

Volkswagen’s third quarter showed the strain behind the restructuring headlines. Revenue slipped from €80,305m to €75,277m and a prior loss of €482m widened to a €4,648m loss, with net margin moving from a small negative at 0.6% to a deeper 6.2% in the red. The bullish profitability story was clearly challenged, so the evidence cut in favour of the cautious case.

The key assumption that moved was margin resilience. For another stock, track whether promised cost cuts show up in net margin, not just in presentations, and compare each new quarter to the old margin path you were told to expect.

sum: Volkswagen's week has been a study in competing pressures. A recall affecting roughly 72,700 electric vehicles, a reported pause on development of the future electric ID. Golf, and a downbeat earnings outlook all landed alongside a EUR 1.95 billion financing move and a mixed set of legal headlines. The common thread: a group trying to fund its electric future while its near-term profitability thins to a sliver.

The recall, reported by media on 2 November, covers models including the ID.3, ID.4, ID.7 and ID. Buzz, plus the Cupra Born. Possible battery defects prompted the action, and until owners bring their cars in for a workshop check, a charging cap of 80% applies. On the development side, Reuters reported that Volkswagen paused work on the upcoming electric ID. Golf so it could first secure the necessary investment, citing an internal message from brand chief Thomas Schäfer.

Those operational headaches sit against a sobering earnings picture. For 2026, the group expects a reported operating return on sales of up to 1%. Strip out special items and the figure comes in around 4%. The reported nine-month operating result collapsed 99% to EUR 0.1 billion, dragged down by negative special effects of EUR 8.7 billion.

Analysts have been adjusting their markers accordingly. JPMorgan cut its price target for the preferred shares from EUR 110 to EUR 85 on 2 November while keeping a "Neutral" rating — a lower target, but no change in its investment verdict. Bernstein Research, meanwhile, resumed coverage of Volkswagen the same day with a "Market-Perform" rating and an EUR 80 target. Analyst Harry Martin pointed to the extensive restructuring as well as investments in products and local manufacturing.

The financing side offered a counterpoint to the gloom. Through its financing arm Volkswagen International Finance N.V., the group raised EUR 1.95 billion by placing two subordinated green hybrid bonds, as Bloomberg reported on Thursday. The capital comes as Audi, the group's premium subsidiary, has secured state subsidies and tax incentives for a planned USD 4 billion plant in Georgia, according to Reuters. Audi is also weighing a second expansion phase, though the construction itself remains a described project and any extension is still under review.

Volkswagen Loosens Its Zero-Wage Playbook as a 1% Margin Leaves Little Room for Error
sum: Volkswagen has quietly widened the goalposts on its global pay policy. According to a Spiegel report published today, a revised internal document now centres on bringing labour costs down to competitive levels, leaving open the possibility of pay rounds with no increases at all. The shift matters to investors for a single reason: whether Europe's biggest carmaker can squeeze out enough savings to steady a business whose profitability has collapsed.

The original instruction, issued in early October, was considerably blunter. Personnel chiefs worldwide were told to push through collective agreements running to 2030 that avoided salary increases wherever possible, while also trimming bonuses, special payments and allowances. That version reached into both base-pay progression and supplementary compensation. The document drafted roughly three weeks later strikes a different tone, focusing on the competitive cost level that zero rounds might help achieve — and making no reference to variable pay. Volkswagen declined to comment on the change, citing the confidentiality of internal papers.

The world works council welcomed the adjustment, a signal that the softer line may find readier acceptance among employees — provided the newly opened room for manoeuvre is actually used. The commercial test, though, remains the cost relief ultimately delivered. What has changed is the emphasis: from individual pay instruments to a target cost level.

The pressure behind that target is easy to see in the numbers. Volkswagen is guiding toward an operating return on sales of at most 1% for 2026, a fraction of the 4–5.5% it once targeted. Restructuring charges, weakness in China and intensifying competition are all weighing on the business, compounded by US tariffs and soft demand.

The nine-month figures published on 29 October lay out the damage. Revenue came in at EUR 233.4 billion, but operating profit reached just EUR 0.1 billion, dragged down by EUR 8.7 billion in special items. For the full year the group expects turnover of around EUR 315 billion. The Brand Group Core, reporting a day later, saw its nine-month operating result slip to EUR 4.33 billion from EUR 4.72 billion a year earlier, with its return on sales falling to 4.1% from 4.4%.

sum: Deutsche Bank has trimmed its price target on Volkswagen's preference shares from EUR 105 to EUR 100 while leaving its buy recommendation in place, a two-speed signal that separates the bank from JPMorgan's more guarded stance on the embattled automaker.

Analyst Tim Rokossa cut the target following a sit-down with VW finance chief Arno Antlitz, an exchange he described as constructive. Talks centered on the ongoing restructuring, cost reduction in Germany and the worsening situation in China. The lower target nonetheless shows that even a positive read on management's plans was not enough to justify an unchanged valuation. The stock added 0.6% in the prior session.

JPMorgan had already moved on Friday, slashing its target from EUR 110 to EUR 85 after the quarterly figures while reaffirming a neutral rating. Media reports pointed to heavy one-off and write-down effects in the most recent quarter as the trigger. Both houses are marking down their valuation expectations; they part ways on what investors should do about it. A reduced target does not amount to a sell call — Deutsche Bank's underlying view stays positive, whereas JPMorgan remains on the sidelines.

The weaker earnings base explains the caution. Volkswagen booked a net loss after tax of EUR 5.8 billion for the third quarter of 2026, dragged down in large part by a non-cash Porsche goodwill impairment of EUR 6.4 billion. That figure cannot be read simply as a verdict on day-to-day operations — but neither does the write-down excuse the operating problems. Earnings power at the core Volkswagen brand remains the key test of the overhaul.

For the first nine months of 2026, the group reported operating profit of EUR 71 million, down from EUR 5,408 million a year earlier. Before special items, operating profit reached EUR 8.8 billion. Management stressed the immediate need for action in light of the nine-month balance sheet. For the full year, Volkswagen expects revenue of around EUR 315 billion and an operating return on sales of up to 1%.
At the brand level, Volkswagen Pkw generated operating profit of EUR 813 million from January to September 2026, a 1.3% operating margin that leaves limited financial headroom.

sum: Rivian RIVN, the electric-vehicle and autonomy developer, climbed 9% to $13.26 at 10:10 a.m. ET on November 2 as UBS upgraded the shares to Buy from Neutral, keeping its $17 target. That gives investors a fresh reason to revisit the company after its recent selloff. The earnings mix still deserves scrutiny: consolidated gross profit is positive, while making vehicles remains a money-losing business.

Rivian's October 29 results put that challenge in numbers. Automotive revenue reached $1.550 billion, producing an $80 million gross loss and an implied gross margin of negative 5.2%. Software and services generated $256 million in gross profit, lifting the consolidated total to $176 million. That segment includes Volkswagen joint-venture development work and repair income, so treating its entire profit as evidence of an autonomy subscription breakthrough would overstate the case.

The GuruFocus snapshot adds a caution flag: Rivian's GF Score of 57 out of 100 combines stronger value and momentum readings with weak profitability and growth readings. The rally may reflect renewed appetite for the opportunity, but sustained progress in vehicle margins remains the key test as R2 scales. December's Autonomy and AI Day could offer another product catalyst; closing the manufacturing profit gap will require evidence from the automotive business itself.

VW's Preferred Shares Caught in the Crossfire as Porsche SE Demands an End to 'Taboos'
sum: The simmering conflict at Volkswagen has escalated into open confrontation, with the company's largest shareholder now publicly demanding that management abandon long-standing taboos around plant closures and job cuts. The Porsche SE holding company, which controls a significant stake in the Wolfsburg-based automaker, has urged the board to seriously consider shuttering facilities to accelerate the pace of restructuring — a move that has dramatically intensified pressure on CEO Oliver Blume's leadership team.

The Porsche SE's intervention comes at a particularly volatile moment. Just days earlier, Volkswagen's supervisory board had rejected the management board's revised austerity package, known as "Group Target Picture 2030," which includes potential plant closures and aims to fundamentally overhaul the company's cost structure. The board's decision to block the plan — at least temporarily — has exposed deep fractures between management and labor representatives, with another supervisory board meeting on the closure plans scheduled for September.

The stakes could hardly be higher. According to a Spiegel report, Volkswagen is considering closing four German plants starting in 2031 — Zwickau and Emden first, followed by Hannover in 2032 and the Audi plant in Neckarsulm in 2034. Manager Magazin has reported that up to 100,000 jobs across the group could be at risk. Works council chief Daniela Cavallo did not mince words in her response to management's approach, telling media that "enough is enough" and that the board's treatment of employees was "beyond disrespectful."

The governance battle unfolds against a backdrop of deteriorating financial performance. Volkswagen reported first-half 2026 earnings per preferred share of EUR 2.56, down sharply from EUR 4.34 in the same period last year. Group deliveries fell 6 percent to 4.1 million vehicles, with Chinese deliveries plunging 37 percent in the second quarter alone. The one bright spot was the Brand Group Core division, which bundles the volume brands: it lifted operating profit 4.5 percent to EUR 3.61 billion, with the operating margin edging up to 4.9 percent.

sum: Europe's largest automaker, Volkswagen Group, slashed its fiscal 2026 earnings outlook for the second time in two months, cutting its full-year operating margin guidance from a previous range of 4.0% to 5.5% to "no more than 1%." The immediate trigger for this warning is spelled out in a regulatory filing Volkswagen published on September 18: a goodwill impairment of approximately €6 billion (approximately $6.9 billion) tied to the Porsche brand, combined with roughly €10 billion (approximately $11.5 billion) in total special items, and expectations of "further significant deterioration" in the China market. On the same day the warning was issued, Volkswagen's supervisory board approved cutting another 4,100 jobs at Porsche to close an indirect cost gap of approximately €700 million (approximately $802.9 million).
Volkswagen shares closed down 5.6% on the news, while Porsche shares fell 3.3%. Porsche SE, Volkswagen's largest shareholder, also lowered its own earnings outlook, with its shares dropping 4.9%.

Porsche's job cuts did not begin today. In March, Porsche CEO Oliver Blume announced a first round of layoffs affecting more than 4,000 positions. In July, Porsche announced another roughly 5,000 job cuts in Germany, to be implemented primarily through attrition, partial retirement, and voluntary separation programs, without forced redundancies. Combined with the newly announced 4,100 positions, total job cuts over the past two years amount to roughly 13,000.

In exchange, Porsche agreed to extend employment guarantees at its Zuffenhausen plant and Weissach R&D center through 2035, and committed to investing €2.1 billion (approximately $2.4 billion) at the two sites. Employees also agreed to defer portions of salary increases totaling 3.5% through 2035.

sum: The arithmetic at Volkswagen is becoming brutally simple: sell off enough peripheral assets to fund a core overhaul before the core's own deterioration eats the proceeds. This week offered fresh evidence that the first half of that equation is moving — the second half remains very much in doubt.

The most concrete step came on Monday, when Porsche signed a binding agreement to offload its IT and management consultancy MHP to Tata Consultancy Services. The Ludwigsburg-based unit employs roughly 4,500 people and generated around €743 million in revenue in 2025. That deal follows hard on the heels of mid-August's EU approval for the sale of a 51% stake in the heavy-engine subsidiary Everllence — formerly MAN Energy Solutions — to Bain Capital for €7.4 billion, a transaction expected to close by the end of 2026.

Two further disposals are reportedly in the pipeline. Volkswagen is said to be preparing a sale of its development arm IAV to Accenture, with a deal targeted before year-end; that transaction would be accompanied by a future-oriented collective agreement that could eliminate more than 2,000 of the roughly 5,000 German jobs at the company. Separately, the group is weighing a reduction of its Traton holding from 87.5% to 75% plus one share — a stake currently worth around €16.6 billion — though timing and scale remain unspecified. The common thread: raising capital without surrendering control of the truck maker.

The pressure to monetize assets is not hard to trace. First-half operating profit came in at €5.9 billion, down 11.6% year-on-year (the secondary source puts the decline at 12%, a rounding difference), on revenue of €158.1 billion. The operating margin stood at 3.8%. China deliveries collapsed by 26% in the half, and by 37% in the second quarter alone — a deterioration that looks increasingly structural rather than cyclical, particularly as local rivals like BYD gain ground even in VW's home market.

The guidance cut on July 24 — with 2026 revenue now expected to fall 3% to 0% and deliveries to decline 3% to 7% — was the formal acknowledgment that the old trajectory was gone. Since that warning, the preferred shares have clawed back 4.8%. The stock closed Thursday at €74.88, up 3.6% on the day, though no single catalyst for that jump was identifiable.

sum: Volkswagen wants the headline to be about jobs. On August 24, labor representatives told employees the restructuring could ultimately touch as many as 140,000 positions, well above the roughly 100,000 management has floated so far. That's a gap of 40,000 people, treated in most of the coverage like a rounding error. It isn't. But it also isn't the real story here.
The real story is sitting in a filing from a different company, one that most of the coverage of Volkswagen's crisis never bothers to open.

On August 7, Porsche Automobil Holding SE, the family holding company through which the Porsche and Piech descendants control Volkswagen, reported a group result after tax of minus 2.2 billion euros for the first half of 2026. The cause was a 3.0 billion euro non-cash impairment on the carrying value of its own Volkswagen AG shares, plus a smaller writedown tied to Porsche AG. In plain English, the family that controls Volkswagen just told its own shareholders, in an audited financial statement, that its stake in the company is worth billions less than it was twelve months ago.

That same filing disclosed something almost as an afterthought. While marking down its core holding, Porsche SE spent the first half of the year adding money to Quantum Motion, Quantum Systems, and Waabi, respectively a quantum-computing hardware startup, a drone and quantum-sensing company, and an autonomous-trucking software firm. Earnings from that side portfolio jumped from 29 million euros to 148 million, and its carrying value now tops 630 million euros.
The people with the most detailed, least filtered view into Volkswagen's finances are writing down the car company and building a venture portfolio that has nothing to do with cars, at the same time.

Start with what actually happened, because it matters on its own terms. Union officials broke the potential 140,000 figure into three layers: about 50,000 reductions already agreed in Germany, another 50,000 spread across the rest of Volkswagen's production network, and roughly 40,000 more tied to the possible closure of four German plants: Emden, Hanover, Zwickau, and Audi's Neckarsulm site.

sum: Two former Volkswagen Group engineers have been arrested and charged in a federal insider trading scheme. The federal indictment alleges the men used non-public corporate data to buy up massive stock positions in EV startup Rivian Automotive just days before VW announced a massive joint venture.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York unsealed the indictment, naming Michael Stamp, 31, and Marcus Plank, 45, as the primary defendants. Both men were German nationals working in California on a temporary assignment for a Volkswagen technology subsidiary. Through their day-to-day access to proprietary powertrain and electronic systems data, they gained early knowledge of the automotive partnership.

While federal prosecutors routinely track suspicious equity spikes through advanced market surveillance algorithms, the case against Stamp and Plank contains a glaring paper trail of digital evidence. According to investigators, the engineers used their personal and work devices to conduct Google searches that directly pointed to their illegal trading plans and anxiety over getting caught.

Some of the incriminating search queries uncovered by the FBI included searches regarding the impending Volkswagen acquisition, the mechanics of insider trading call options, how the SEC catches insider traders, and whether the FBI can track deleted search history.

Despite their apparent concerns, the pair proceeded with the strategy. Shortly after learning of the partnership discussions, the pair began aggressively purchasing high-leverage short-term call options and standard equity positions in Rivian stock.
When Volkswagen officially made the joint venture public, Rivian shares skyrocketed. The sudden market spike triggered the engineers' option contracts, netting them huge, immediate returns.

Stamp pocketed approximately $250,000 in illegal gains and immediately began transferring the funds to his personal bank accounts, while Plank walked away with at least $50,000 after liquidating his option contracts. Additionally, Plank allegedly tipped off a family member who managed to squeeze out $12,000 from the stock movement.

Volkswagen was supposed to manufacture components for the Iron Dome. A shareholder from Qatar blocked the deal
sum: Recent years have not been kind to the German automotive giant. The difficult and costly transition from internal combustion engines to electric vehicles, combined with growing problems stemming from the mass influx of cheaper Chinese competition into Europe, has forced the group known for Beetles, Golfs, and Passats to seek alternative revenue sources. The global geopolitical situation prompted the Germans to open up to the broadly defined defence industry.

One manifestation of this opening was the collaboration with the Israeli defence company Rafael (Rafael Advanced Defence Systems) announced earlier this year. Joint activities were to be based on the production of components for „Iron Dome” anti-missile systems at the Volkswagen factory in Osnabrück, where car production is scheduled to end this year. The partnership was intended to satisfy both parties – the German side would prevent mass layoffs and the factory’s closure, while the Israeli entity would diversify its production, a move justified by security concerns given the tense situation in the Middle East. Under a letter of intent signed in April, the German automotive company committed not only to producing trucks to transport components of the Israeli system but also, among other things, to the production of power generators.

In July, it turned out that these investments will likely not materialize. This is due to a minority shareholder in Volkswagen—the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA)—which reportedly blocked the cooperation in Osnabrück. The main reason? Qatari policy toward Israel. An additional blocking factor was the labor unions within the company itself, which also protested against producing for an Israeli firm famous for its Trophy APS (Active Protection System) and Spike anti-tank missiles.

Despite the fact that Porsche SE holds more than 50 percent of the company’s shares and QIA is a minority investor (approximately 10 percent), Volkswagen management decided to respect the Qatari blockade. This decision stems not only from financial considerations (fears of losing a shareholder) but also from the aforementioned protests by some employees and local activists who want the factory in the German city to remain focused exclusively on production for the civilian market.

sum: The biggest single-day market cap gain in stock market history belongs to NVIDIA, which added roughly $329 billion in value on July 31, 2024. That one trading session created more wealth than the entire market capitalization of companies like McDonald’s or Disney, and it did so in under seven hours.

This figure is not a fluke. It is the product of a specific structural shift: when a company is worth $3 trillion or more, a routine 5% to 10% move translates into hundreds of billions of dollars. Nine of the ten largest single-day gains on record happened in 2024 alone, and every one of them involves a US technology company. This article ranks the largest gains, explains why they cluster in the AI era, and covers the data points most competing lists leave out, including the record losses that are the mirror image of these gains.

Definition Box A single-day market cap gain is the dollar increase in a company’s total market value between one trading day’s close and the next. It is calculated as the change in share price multiplied by shares outstanding. It is distinct from a percentage gain (the proportional move, which favors smaller or more volatile stocks) and from an index point gain (which measures a whole benchmark like the Dow, not a single company).

NVIDIA holds the record with approximately $329 billion added on July 31, 2024. The chipmaker’s shares jumped nearly 13% in a single session, lifted by optimism over AI chip demand after Microsoft signaled rising capital expenditure and rival AMD posted strong results. The gain blasted past NVIDIA’s own previous record of roughly $277 billion, set in February 2024.

A note on precision: exact figures vary by a few billion dollars depending on the data provider, because shares outstanding and closing prices are sourced differently across LSEG, Bloomberg, and Yahoo Finance. sum: A target of 19,000 fewer German workers by the close of 2026 is part of the restructuring plan Volkswagen AG is executing, according to remarks delivered by CEO Oliver Blume to shareholders at the June 18 annual general meeting.

The cuts apply to Volkswagen AG, including its Sachsen and Osnabrück plants. Across Volkswagen, Audi, Porsche, and software subsidiary CARIAD, signed departure agreements now cover more than 28,000 employees through 2030 — a milestone within the group's wider goal of shedding roughly 50,000 positions at its German facilities by that year.

The automaker said it cut factory costs at Volkswagen's German sites by more than 20 percent in 2025. Through collective bargaining agreements and headcount reductions, the company said it has achieved sustainable cost savings of around 1 billion euros across the group to date, working toward annual net savings of 6 billion euros by 2030.

Blume said the job reductions are driven by the need to bring production capacity in line with current demand. Volkswagen had built a global production network based on an annual capacity of 12 million vehicles, a figure set before the COVID pandemic on more optimistic assumptions. The company now considers roughly 9 million vehicles — its average over the past five years — a realistic target, and said it has already removed some 2 million units of capacity from its European and Chinese production network over the past two years.

The company posted an operating result of approximately 8.9 billion euros in 2025, with a margin of 2.8 percent, weighed down by nearly 9 billion euros in one-off special effects and U.S. tariff costs. Volkswagen delivered roughly 9 million vehicles worldwide that year, with sales revenue of around 322 billion euros.

Looking ahead, Blume said Volkswagen expects an operating return on sales of between 4 and 5.5 percent for 2026 and net cash flow in the automotive division of between 3 and 6 billion euros. The company's long-term ambition is an operating return on sales of 8 to 10 percent by 2030.

Tariffs continue to weigh on the business, Blume said, with a negative effect of around 5 billion euros per year through direct and indirect impacts, particularly on exports from Europe and products from Mexico.

sum: Volkswagen now owns 209.8 million shares of Rivian (RIVN), representing a 15.9% stake in the EV startup, according to a new SEC filing. The German automaker has overtaken Amazon as Rivian’s single largest shareholder for the first time since the company’s 2021 IPO.

The stake increase came after Volkswagen’s US subsidiary purchased 62.9 million new shares on April 30 at $15.90 per share — a roughly $1 billion investment triggered by the joint venture hitting its latest testing milestone.

The $1 billion share purchase is the latest tranche under the up to $5.8 billion investment agreement that VW and Rivian signed in November 2024. The deal structures VW’s investment in $1 billion increments, each contingent on the Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies (RV Tech) joint venture hitting specific milestones.

This particular tranche was unlocked after the joint venture completed winter testing of its production-intent zonal architecture for first-generation software-defined vehicles. Prototype vehicles from VW, Audi, and Scout Motors all passed the validation, clearing the way for VW to cut the check.

Including this latest purchase, VW has now deployed roughly $3.3 billion of its $5.8 billion commitment to Rivian — an initial $1 billion convertible note in mid-2024, approximately $1.3 billion at the joint venture’s launch for background IP licenses and equity, and now this latest $1 billion equity tranche.

Amazon held approximately 158.4 million Rivian shares heading into the transaction. Before VW’s latest purchase, Amazon was still Rivian’s top outside investor — a position it held since leading Rivian’s $700 million funding round in 2019.

But the April 30 share issuance changed the math. VW now holds 209.8 million shares (15.9%) compared to Amazon’s roughly 158.4 million shares, which have been diluted to approximately 11.8% of the expanded share count. Amazon’s stake has eroded from about 20% at the time of Rivian’s IPO to under 12% today, entirely through dilution — Amazon hasn’t sold a single share.

sum: With Terafab in focus and deliveries disappointing, April 22 forces investors to decide what Tesla actually is.

Tesla reports Q1 2026 results on April 22 after the U.S. close. The stock enters earnings week having just broken out of a multi-month descending channel, up over 7% on an AI chip development announcement - but the underlying fundamentals tell a more complicated story. Deliveries already came in below expectations, margins are under pressure, and investors are increasingly trying to price a company that may be in the early stages of leaving the auto business behind.

Street consensus sits around EPS of $0.37 on revenue of $22.71 billion, though Refinitiv's Smart Estimate is more cautious at $0.30 EPS / $21.52B revenue, with a predicted earnings surprise of –20.6%. The gap between the Wall Street headline and the model-implied downside is itself a signal worth watching.

The most consequential number on April 22 may not be EPS - it may be the incremental capital expenditure commentary around Terafab. Tesla's 2026 capex guide already exceeded $20 billion, but Terafab - the planned 1-terawatt AI compute facility - was explicitly excluded from that figure. If fully realised, Terafab could cost in the mid-single-digit trillions, a number that dwarfs Tesla's entire automotive revenue base. sum: In 1998, Volkswagen Group believed it had pulled off one of the most audacious coups in automotive history. For roughly $790 million, VW emerged as the winning bidder for Rolls-Royce Motor Cars, seemingly securing one of the most prestigious names ever to grace a hood ornament. The deal looked bulletproof on paper: the legendary Crewe factory, the rights to iconic vehicle designs, and even the Spirit of Ecstasy mascot appeared to be safely in Volkswagen’s grasp. To Wolfsburg executives, it felt like a decisive leap into the ultra-luxury stratosphere, instantly elevating VW’s brand portfolio beyond Audi.

But within months, a stunning reality emerged. Volkswagen had bought almost everything associated with cars, except the Rolls-Royce name itself. That priceless trademark was controlled not by the car company, but by Rolls-Royce plc, the aerospace firm, which quietly licensed it to BMW. What followed was one of the most extraordinary corporate miscalculations in automotive history, proving that in the luxury world, identity can be worth far more than bricks, machinery, or even heritage-filled factories.

Volkswagen entered the late 1990s on an acquisition spree, aggressively expanding its brand empire. Ferdinand Piëch, then chairman of VW Group, envisioned a portfolio that spanned from humble city cars to the most opulent limousines on Earth. When Vickers, the parent company of Rolls-Royce Motor Cars, put the business up for sale, VW saw a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. A bidding war ensued with BMW, already a key supplier of engines and electronics to Rolls-Royce and Bentley.

VW ultimately outbid BMW with an offer of around $790 million, a figure that stunned industry observers at the time. From Volkswagen’s perspective, this wasn’t just about profits; it was about prestige. Rolls-Royce was the pinnacle of automotive luxury, a brand synonymous with wealth, power, and near-mythical craftsmanship. Owning it would instantly crown VW as a serious rival to Mercedes-Benz at the very top of the market.
The problem was that VW assumed the Rolls-Royce name came bundled with the car company. In reality, the trademark was owned separately by Rolls-Royce plc, the jet engine manufacturer.

Volkswagen Passat Estate review: Second place in the space race
sum: Volkswagen has celebrated several big birthdays in recent years, with both the Polo supermini and Golf hatchback marking their 50th anniversaries. Yet the Passat, first launched in 1973, seemingly did not merit a special commemorative edition when it turned 50.

Volkswagen has launched a new version of the Passat, though, now only available in estate guise for European customers. The declining popularity of four-door saloons probably makes this a wise decision, but estate cars have also suffered greatly at the hands of the all-conquering SUV.

Sensibly, Volkswagen pursued economies of scale when developing the new Passat. Not only does this latest model use the same platform and powertrains as the Skoda Superb, it even shares the same production facility in Bratislava, Slovakia.

It means the closest competition for the Passat comes from within, as the Superb Estate undercuts its German brother on price. Yet the Volkswagen’s upmarket badge could also see it face off against alternatives like the BMW 3 Series Touring and Mercedes-Benz C-Class Estate, plus an endless array of family SUVs.
Although the Passat owes much to the Skoda Superb, Volkswagen’s design team has made it look distinct from its Czech relation.

The result is a handsome, if slightly anodyne estate car, but one with an impressive 0.25 drag coefficient. It means the big wagon cuts through the air cleanly, and is actually the most aerodynamic petrol-powered Volkswagen estate to date.

Another major change is the total absence of diesel engines for the UK market. Estates and the black pump have had a long-term relationship, but Volkswagen has opted for petrol engines only this time.
